reference.source: GeneReviews Rhizomelic Chondrodysplasia Punctata / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: The clinical hallmark is symmetrical rhizomelic (proximal) shortening of the limbs, particularly the humeri and femora, with early cataracts and profound developmental delay

It is an autosomal recessive peroxisomal disorder, most often from PEX7 mutations (type 1) affecting the peroxisomal targeting-2 import pathway, and less often from GNPAT or AGPS defects (types 2 and 3)
The unifying biochemical defect is deficient synthesis of plasmalogens, a class of ether phospholipids essential for membranes and myelin
In PEX7-related disease phytanic acid alpha-oxidation is also impaired, so plasma phytanic acid can be elevated while very-long-chain fatty acids remain normal
Radiographs show punctate epiphyseal calcification (chondrodysplasia punctata) and coronal clefts of the vertebral bodies
Seizures, joint contractures, feeding difficulty, recurrent respiratory infections and characteristic facial features are common

Care is supportive, addressing feeding, respiratory infection, seizures, orthopaedic contractures and cataracts, with generic dietary phytanic-acid restriction considered where phytanic acid is raised
reference.pathophysiology: Rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata is a disorder of peroxisomal metabolism in which the import or activity of a small group of peroxisomal enzymes is disrupted. In the common PEX7 form, the receptor for the peroxisomal targeting signal 2 fails, so enzymes bearing that signal, including those for plasmalogen biosynthesis and phytanic acid alpha-oxidation, are not correctly delivered to the peroxisome. Types 2 and 3 involve direct deficiency of the plasmalogen synthetic enzymes encoded by GNPAT and AGPS. The shared consequence is severely deficient plasmalogen synthesis, which impairs formation of myelin and other specialised membranes; accumulation of phytanic acid contributes in the PEX7 form. These defects underlie the skeletal, ocular and neurological features.
additionalDifferentials: Warfarin embryopathy and maternal vitamin K deficiency effects
Classic Refsum disease (also PEX7-related, high phytanic acid)
Achondroplasia and other rhizomelic skeletal dysplasias
additionalInvestigations: Erythrocyte plasmalogen levels, which are reduced
Plasma phytanic acid (may be elevated) with normal very-long-chain fatty acids
Skeletal radiographs demonstrating punctate epiphyseal calcification and vertebral coronal clefts
Molecular genetic testing of PEX7, GNPAT and AGPS
Brain MRI and EEG to assess myelination and seizures
redFlags: Recurrent aspiration or respiratory infection compromising ventilation
Severe feeding failure and failure to thrive
Rapid clinical deterioration in the neonatal or infantile period
reference.prognosis: The classic form carries a poor prognosis with severe developmental impairment and reduced survival, many affected children not surviving early childhood, although milder variants with residual enzyme function can survive longer with a less severe course.
pitfalls: Mistaking the punctate calcification for warfarin embryopathy or X-linked chondrodysplasia punctata without biochemical testing
Checking only very-long-chain fatty acids, which are normal, and missing the low plasmalogens that establish the diagnosis
Overlooking treatable contributors such as elevated phytanic acid in the PEX7 form
Failing to arrange early cataract assessment and airway or feeding support
management: Supportive care as there is no curative therapy, with anticonvulsants to control the frequent seizures
Consider dietary phytanic-acid restriction in the PEX7 form to limit phytanate accumulation
Nutritional support for feeding difficulty, including gastrostomy feeding where swallowing is unsafe
Proactive respiratory management with prompt treatment of recurrent chest infections and ventilatory support as needed
Cataract extraction and ophthalmological follow-up for the congenital cataracts
Physiotherapy, orthotics and orthopaedic care for joint contractures, rhizomelic deformity and spasticity
Coordinated metabolic, neurology, ophthalmology and palliative-care input given the poor prognosis
Genetic counselling with carrier and prenatal testing for this autosomal recessive disorder
